**Short version**

A TLB (translation lookaside buffer) is a small cache in each CPU core that stores recent virtual-to-physical address translations. On a server with hundreds of GB of memory, the TLB covers only a few MB when pages are 4 KB, so many memory accesses need a slow lookup in the page tables. Huge pages (2 MB or 1 GB) make each TLB entry cover 512 or 262,144 times more memory, but they can reserve or waste memory, cause long pauses during allocation, and give no gain to workloads that the TLB did not limit.

## 1. What a TLB is

- A program uses virtual addresses. The CPU must translate each one to a physical address (the real location in memory) before it can read or write.
- The operating system keeps the mapping in page tables. Memory is divided into pages of 4 KB by default, and each page has one 8-byte entry.
- On x86-64 the page table is a tree with 4 levels, or 5 levels on CPUs with 57-bit addresses [Ref1].
- The TLB stores the results of recent translations. A hit (the translation is in the TLB) adds almost no time.
- A miss forces a page walk: the CPU reads one entry at each level of the tree. Each read needs the result of the previous one.

```
virtual address --> [ TLB ] --hit--> physical address
                       |
                      miss
                       v
       [L4] --> [L3] --> [L2] --> [L1] --> physical address
       page walk: up to 4 memory reads, one after another
```

A Skylake-generation Xeon core has 64 entries in its first-level data TLB and 1,536 entries in its second-level TLB [Ref2]. Newer cores have about 2,000 (est.); `cpuid -1` on the target machine gives the exact counts.

## 2. Why misses are expensive on a big-memory server

- **Coverage is very small.** 1,536 entries x 4 KB = 6 MB, which is about 0.001% of a 512 GB server. A workload that reads a large heap in random order misses on nearly every access.
- **The page tables do not fit in the CPU cache.** Mapping 512 GB with 4 KB pages needs 134 million entries, which is 1 GB of last-level page tables. The CPU cache holds tens of MB to about 100 MB (est.). The last read of the walk must often come from main memory (DRAM), which takes about 100 ns (est., about 300 cycles at 3 GHz).
- **The data read often misses too.** One load then costs two DRAM accesses instead of one.
- **Multi-socket servers add distance.** With NUMA (non-uniform memory access: each socket has its own memory, and the other socket's memory is slower to reach), the page tables can sit on the other socket.
- **Virtual machines translate twice.** One miss can need up to 24 memory reads [Ref3].
- **Measured scale.** One study ran graph500 (a graph-search benchmark) on a 2013 Xeon server. TLB misses took 51% of execution cycles with 4 KB pages, 10% with 2 MB pages, and 1.5% with 1 GB pages [Ref4]. The hardware is old, so this shows the size of the effect, not a prediction.

## 3. How huge pages help

| Page size | Second-level TLB covers (Skylake Xeon) | Last-level page tables for 512 GB | Page-walk reads (max) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4 KB | 1,536 entries = 6 MB | 1 GB | 4 |
| 2 MB | 1,536 entries = 3 GB | 2 MB | 3 |
| 1 GB | 16 entries = 16 GB | 4 KB | 2 |

Newer cores have many more 1 GB entries: about 1,000 (est.; confirm with `cpuid -1`).

- **Fewer misses.** Each entry covers 512 times (2 MB) or 262,144 times (1 GB) more memory.
- **Cheaper misses.** The walk is one or two levels shorter, and the page tables are small enough to stay in the CPU cache.
- **Fewer page faults.** A page fault is the kernel work that maps a page on first access. One fault maps 2 MB instead of 512 separate 4 KB faults.

Linux offers two mechanisms:

- **Reserved huge pages** (hugetlbfs, the explicit kernel interface). The administrator reserves a fixed number of 2 MB or 1 GB pages, and the application must request them [Ref5].
- **THP** (Transparent Huge Pages). The kernel uses 2 MB pages for ordinary application memory with no application change. A kernel thread named khugepaged merges 4 KB pages into 2 MB pages in the background. The modes are `always`, `madvise` (only regions the application marks), and `never` [Ref6].

## 4. What can go wrong

**Reserved huge pages**

- **Reserved memory is lost to everything else.** The file cache and other processes cannot use it, even when the application leaves it idle. On a shared server this reduces the memory of the other users.
- **A reservation that is too small fails the application.** The allocation returns an error, or the process is killed with SIGBUS (the bus-error signal) when no huge page is free [Ref5].
- **A late reservation can fail.** The kernel needs contiguous free physical memory. After long uptime the memory is fragmented, and the kernel grants fewer pages than requested. Reserve 1 GB pages on the kernel command line at boot [Ref5].
- **The reservation is split across sockets.** A process bound to one socket can find no free huge pages while the other socket still has some [Ref5].
- **Memory monitoring under-reports.** These pages are not counted in RSS (resident set size, the usual per-process memory figure). They appear in the separate `HugetlbPages` field of `/proc/PID/status` [Ref5].

**THP**

- **Long pauses at allocation.** When no free 2 MB block exists, the kernel may compact memory (move pages to create a contiguous block) inside the application's page fault. The thread stops for milliseconds (est.). The `defrag` setting controls this behavior [Ref6].
- **Memory use grows.** An application that touches 1 byte receives a whole 2 MB page. Allocator libraries that return memory in 4 KB pieces (jemalloc, tcmalloc) work poorly with this.
- **First access is slower.** The kernel clears the whole 2 MB first, which takes 100 to 200 us (est.), against about 1 us (est.) for a 4 KB page.
- **Fork becomes expensive.** After fork (the system call that creates a child process sharing the parent's memory), the first write to a shared page forces a copy. With THP the unit is 2 MB instead of 4 KB. Redis documents large latency and memory growth during snapshots for this reason [Ref7].
- **The gain can disappear without an error message.** A partial `munmap`, `mprotect`, or `madvise` on a 2 MB page makes the kernel split it into 4 KB pages. When memory is fragmented, the kernel uses 4 KB pages instead. Check `AnonHugePages` in `/proc/meminfo` and `thp_fault_fallback` in `/proc/vmstat` [Ref6].

**Both mechanisms**

- **No gain when TLB misses were not the limit.** Sequential access and small working sets already hit the TLB.
- **Some CPUs have fewer TLB entries for huge pages.** Skylake has 32 first-level entries for 2 MB pages against 64 for 4 KB pages, and 4 for 1 GB pages [Ref2]. A workload that reads many scattered huge pages still misses.
- **Virtual machines need huge pages in both guest and host** to get the full gain.

## 5. Measurements to bring to the review

- **Before:** run `perf stat` (the Linux performance counter tool) with `dTLB-load-misses`, `dTLB-loads`, `cycles`, and the Intel event `dtlb_load_misses.walk_active` (cycles in which a page walk was running). The share `walk_active / cycles` is roughly the largest speed-up that fewer TLB misses can give.
- **After:** read the same counters, and run `grep -i huge /proc/meminfo` to confirm the huge pages are in use.

## References

- [Ref1] Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual, Volume 3A, chapter "Paging", including the section "Caching Translation Information".
- [Ref2] Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Optimization Reference Manual, Skylake microarchitecture, TLB parameters table.
- [Ref3] Bhargava et al., "Accelerating Two-Dimensional Page Walks for Virtualized Systems", ASPLOS 2008.
- [Ref4] Basu et al., "Efficient Virtual Memory for Big Memory Servers", ISCA 2013.
- [Ref5] Linux kernel documentation, "HugeTLB Pages", https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/mm/hugetlbpage.html
- [Ref6] Linux kernel documentation, "Transparent Hugepage Support", https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/mm/transhuge.html
- [Ref7] Redis documentation, "Diagnosing latency issues", section "Latency induced by transparent huge pages".
